intros.market: Five certificate authorities control 91.65% of all publicly trusted TLS certificates, with Internet Security Research Group (Let's Encrypt) commanding 38.7% and Google Trust Services holding 20.9%. The top three CAs account for 74.04% of issuance, producing an HHI of 2324, which signals moderate concentration. Meanwhile, 75 CAs in the long tail collectively issue less than 9% of certificates but retain full trust store inclusion across all major browsers.
intros.trust: The four major trust stores collectively contain 335 roots from 89 CA owners, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores simultaneously. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating significant operational divergence. Only 38 CA owners are trusted across all four programs, meaning certificate chains validated by one browser may fail in another, forcing CAs to maintain parallel hierarchies and complicating incident response when distrust decisions diverge.
intros.conc: The WebPKI exhibits systemic dependency on a handful of operators, with the top five CAs issuing 91.65% of all certificates and an HHI of 2324 indicating moderate but growing concentration. Let's Encrypt alone represents 38.7% of the ecosystem, meaning a single operational failure or distrust event at ISRG would immediately affect more than one-third of the encrypted web. This concentration sits atop a governance layer where only 21 of 56 CA/B Forum members actively contribute to policy development, compounding the risk that a small number of entities shape both issuance and rule-making.
intros.tail: Seventy-five certificate authorities collectively issue just 8.35% of publicly trusted certificates yet maintain full inclusion in major trust stores, creating asymmetric risk. These low-volume CAs face the same 6,664 regulatory obligations as high-volume operators but lack the engineering resources and incident detection systems demonstrated by the top five. The tail accounts for a disproportionate share of governance and misissuance incidents, with 54 CAs responsible for 1,545 documented compliance failures while browsers provide oversight comments on only 5.4% to 18.4% of reported issues in 2025.
intros.geo: United States-incorporated CAs issue 91.46% of all publicly trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of 89 trusted authorities, while 44 European CAs collectively account for 8.45% and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs issue just 0.08%. This geographic concentration means the WebPKI's operational resilience depends almost entirely on US-based entities and US legal jurisdiction. The imbalance also shapes governance dynamics, with Chrome and Mozilla providing substantially higher oversight coverage than other programs while Apple and Microsoft defer to audit letters that catch only 31% of in-scope incidents.
intros.gov: Thirty state-operated or state-owned certificate authorities hold trusted roots across major browsers, issuing 0.07% of all certificates but retaining the technical capability to impersonate any domain within their trust scope. These government CAs span jurisdictions including China, Russia, India, Turkey, and multiple European nations, creating geopolitical surface area where compelled disclosure laws intersect with cryptographic trust. Unlike commercial CAs subject to market discipline and distrust threat, government operators face minimal competitive pressure and often operate under legal frameworks that mandate domestic interception capabilities.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled disclosure or interception mandates, including China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong, with India and Turkey designated moderate-risk. CAs incorporated in these regions face legal frameworks that may compel key disclosure, require law enforcement access, or prohibit public disclosure of government demands. The 30 government-operated CAs overlap substantially with high-risk jurisdictions, and 142 Microsoft-only roots create opacity around which authorities hold trusted status outside the three transparent root programs.
intros.ops: Certificate authorities have reported 1,545 compliance incidents across 54 organizations, with misissuance accounting for 601 events and governance failures for 495. Only 26% of incidents are self-detected by the issuing CA, while 19% are found by external researchers and just 8% by auditors, indicating weak internal controls. Policy failures (188 incidents) and disclosure failures (137 incidents) together represent 21% of the total, suggesting CAs struggle not only with technical compliance but with transparency obligations and baseline procedural discipline.
intros.crypto: Root certificate algorithms and key sizes across the 335 trusted roots show legacy cryptographic posture, with multiple programs still trusting SHA-1 intermediate capability and 1024-bit DSA roots despite known weaknesses. The transition to post-quantum algorithms remains entirely absent from production hierarchies as of August 2026. Key agility is limited by the median 1,185-day runway granted during distrust events, meaning cryptographic migrations require multi-year coordination across browser vendors, CAs, and subscriber populations.
intros.distrust: Browsers have executed 16 full distrust events against certificate authorities, with 14 stemming from compliance or operational failures and 10 following a demonstrated pattern of repeated issues. The plurality of distrusted CAs exhibited negligent noncompliance (7 cases) or demonstrated incompetence (3 cases), while 3 involved willful circumvention of baseline requirements. The median 1,185-day distrust runway reflects browsers' reluctance to disrupt subscriber certificates, but this grace period also allows failing CAs to remain trusted for more than three years after terminal incidents, during which they continue issuing to new subscribers.
intros.policy: Forty-three active TLS issuers face compressed certificate validity limits under SC-081, with only 9 CAs demonstrating actual replacement behavior at or below the March 2029 target of 47 days while 4 remain at risk of non-compliance even with the March 2026 200-day threshold. The regulatory obligations CAs must navigate have grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,664 total requirements, with 76% classified as mandatory across CA/B Forum baselines, root program policies, WebTrust/ETSI criteria, and IETF/NIST standards. Zero CA/B Forum ballots have passed since 2022 to rationalize or consolidate this expanding surface, meaning compliance complexity increases while operational readiness declines.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67.8% (Chrome) and 78.0% (Mozilla) of reported incidents in 2019 to just 18.4% and 9.9% respectively in 2025, while Apple provides substantive comments on only 5.4% and Microsoft on 0.0%. Across 1,830 Bugzilla incidents tracked, Chrome has contributed substantive analysis to 293 cases and Mozilla to 249, but recent engagement has dropped to 112 and 47 substantive comments respectively. This governance void means the majority of CA compliance failures receive no public root program scrutiny, leaving audit letters as the sole oversight mechanism despite their 31% in-period detection rate.
intros.community: The CA/B Forum has 56 members, but only 21 contribute actively to policy development while 35 maintain zero participation in ballot or discussion processes. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, with Sectigo also leading organizational participation across working groups. Zero ballots have passed since 2022 to address the 6,664-obligation regulatory surface or the declining governance oversight that now covers under 10% of Mozilla incidents, indicating structural paralysis in the primary standards body responsible for baseline requirements.
intros.audit: WebTrust and ETSI audit letters report a 31% in-period detection rate, meaning auditors identified only 128 of the 414 in-scope compliance incidents that occurred during their examination windows. Thirty-eight CAs exhibit high transparency gaps between clean audit opinions and documented Bugzilla incident histories, while only 4 letters contain qualified opinions and 9 reference the ETSI EN 319 411-2 v3.5 standard adopted in 2025. CAs self-report 58.8% of WebTrust findings and 66.1% of ETSI findings, indicating audit letters function more as compliance attestation than independent surveillance, leaving external researchers and root programs to detect the majority of operational failures after issuance.
